questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to visit an English speaking to improve both my professional and casual English skills.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UBC Go Global made it easy to find and get help - something KU could learn from. They actually had a walk-in office with actual people you could talk to, not just a phone to call. WILD!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Help to find a new course, when my first course was meant for other students than me.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: "Imagine Day" - the first day on campus was a bit tame, and they did not have enough food even though they told us not to bring lunch

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was okay to find, but SO expensive. We payed almost 8000 kr pr person, and i didn't even have my own room. Vancouver is ridiculous

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The buses public transport in Vancouver is mostly great, but the majority of social interactions happened between people on campus, so i felt a bit left out because i lived so far off

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Didn't get offered housing, so i was disappointed by that, but the offered housing was okay. They required each student to get their own pans, pots, cutlery, pillows and duvés, which seemed like a bit of a waste since most people throw it out after they leave.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Tedious, and very little information about each course. 
As a master's student, it was super laborious to actually getting permission to do gradiuate (500) level courses, requiring you to mail professors for permission, none of which replied to my mails. Additionally, the courses only have 1-2 sentences about the content available prior to enrollment, so you have no idea what you're signing up to. I had to change courses twice because the courses i got accepted to were either way too easy or aimed at other study-programmes

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: If you knew which course you wanted to change, you could talk to GoGlobal, which were very helpful, and available throughout the entire schoolday in the first few weeks. Zoom presentation about course registration prior to departure.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: 5/10, i didn't get permission to attend any of the graduate(500) level courses i wanted to attend.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just pick something, and change later, it's a lottery which courses you get, and which ones actually make sense for you to take, and most courses open up for switching around in the first two weeks anyway. unless you're computer science, then good luck.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had courses that were more demanding then in DK, and some that were much less demanding, both of them 400 level. The focus is very different than in Denmark, so if you like memorizing useless information that you forget a week after your exam, then studying in Canada is for you. On a serious note, the course level was very appropriate, but many courses had a very large course load in terms of home-assignments.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I had both lectures and class teaching. Lectures were very concise but had great content. Class teaching felt a bit like danish high-school, with many questions, many of them a bit superfluous.
Overall a much larger focus on memorization, something i found very annoying and not very useful. Less focus on translating what you learn into a project setting like we focus on in Denmark, more just memorizing what's on the slides or in the text.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
BIOC402 Protein structure and function
BIOL440 Plant genomics
BINF548 Directed studies (similar to projekt udenfor kursusregi)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: BIOC402 (Protein structure and function) was a great but tough course, but gives you ALL information you will need to work with or study proteins. Dives deep into protein folding, interactions, structure determination and functional studies at a high level, but they are good at building your knowledge up from not knowing a lot. Probably in the top 3 uni-course i've taken in my 5 years of study.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Club memberships, accidentally spent 200 kroner calling a US number because i didn't understand their phone# system.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food shopping is very expensive, like considerably more expensive than in DK, if you shop in supermarkets. I did the majority of my shopping in a local Korean shop (Kim's Mart on Broadway), which was considerably LESS expensive than supermarkets in DK. Shop in non-chain supermarkets and save! 

Beer/alcohol is less expensive in restaurants/fancy bars, but more expensive in Liquor stores. 
Coffee is also less expensive than in Copenhagen

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: So many clubs, it's crazy

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Pretty much everything you could imagine. 
Every club from rowing, hockey, football, American football, swimming (all of these free), to skiing, hiking, horse riding, engineering (boats, rockets, robots), gaming, smoking cannabis and speaking mandarin. SO MANY

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking-club offered free rentals of different equipment. Many were in the ski/surf club, though they were very poorly organized, and the organizers were very self-absorbed and just liked attention. An example was making people wanting a CHANCE to get tickets to a ski-trip run into the water at the beach in their clothes, most of them not ending up getting one. They seemed like jerks.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Hike, hike some more, then do a hike, and after that you can hike.
Vancouver Island is my new favorite place on earth. Go to the rockies as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Say thank you when leaving the bus, and expect to have strangers striking conversation with you at every conceivable moment. Vancouverites are very friendly!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Do a project, or talk to people in class, though i didn't manage to talk to many.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The amount of homeless people in Vancouver was quite a shock, and tipping. Tipping is the root to all evil, just pay your employees a fair salary.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and kindness from strangers was heartwarming.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go on hikes
Go to Vancouver Island
Don't cry if you don't see a bear, though you probably will, they are friendly, but carry a spray in your group.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Stay on campus if you're offered.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Hiking

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding friends, but stay on campus and it'll be no problem.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go hiking

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
